reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: Defined by bilateral absence of the radii with characteristically preserved thumbs, an important distinction from Fanconi anaemia in which thumbs are typically abnormal
Thrombocytopenia is present from birth or early infancy and is usually most severe in the first year, then tends to improve with age
Most cases involve a low-frequency null allele of RBM8A together with a common hypomorphic non-coding variant on the other allele, giving a compound inheritance pattern
Cow's milk protein intolerance can precipitate acute drops in the platelet count and gastrointestinal symptoms
Other skeletal and cardiac anomalies may accompany the radial defect, but the humeri and thumbs are relatively spared
Bleeding risk is greatest in infancy and platelet transfusion support is used for significant haemorrhage or before procedures
Diagnosis rests on the clinical combination of radial aplasia with preserved thumbs plus thrombocytopenia, confirmed by RBM8A analysis
reference.pathophysiology: TAR syndrome is a disorder of megakaryopoiesis and limb development linked to reduced function of RBM8A, a gene encoding a core component of the exon junction complex that regulates messenger RNA processing. Affected individuals typically inherit a rare loss-of-function allele on one chromosome and a common low-expressing regulatory variant on the other, so the gene product is insufficient in the tissues that depend most on it. The resulting deficiency impairs megakaryocyte production and maturation, producing a hypomegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, while parallel effects on limb morphogenesis cause bilateral radial aplasia with sparing of the thumbs. Unlike the classic inherited bone-marrow failure syndromes, the thrombocytopenia is usually isolated and tends to remit over the first years of life rather than progressing to pancytopenia.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi anaemia (radial anomalies with absent or hypoplastic thumbs)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film confirming thrombocytopenia with otherwise preserved lineages
Bone marrow examination showing reduced or absent megakaryocytes
Upper limb and skeletal radiographs documenting radial aplasia with preserved thumbs
RBM8A molecular analysis including the null allele and the common non-coding variant
Echocardiography and renal imaging for associated anomalies
Chromosome breakage testing where Fanconi anaemia needs to be excluded
redFlags: Significant haemorrhage, including intracranial bleeding, during the high-risk first year of life
Acute fall in platelet count associated with cow's milk exposure or intercurrent infection
Evolving pancytopenia, which should prompt reconsideration of an alternative marrow-failure diagnosis
Abnormal thumbs or positive chromosome breakage suggesting Fanconi anaemia instead
reference.prognosis: The thrombocytopenia is typically most dangerous in infancy and generally improves toward near-normal platelet counts in later childhood, so with careful support through the early high-risk period the long-term haematological outlook is good.
pitfalls: Confusing TAR with Fanconi anaemia; checking the thumbs and performing breakage testing avoids this error
Overlooking cow's milk protein intolerance as a trigger for acute thrombocytopenic episodes
Assuming persistent severe thrombocytopenia, when counts usually improve over time
Neglecting associated cardiac or renal anomalies during the neonatal assessment
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
